analysis.investment_thesis: Stanbik Agro fails the Magic Formula on the quality dimension — ROE of 0.38% implies near-zero return on capital, which disqualifies it regardless of price. A P/E of 11.9 is not cheap enough to compensate for a commodity-trading business earning essentially nothing on its asset base.
key_strengths: P/E of 11.9 is moderate, not extreme (earnings yield ~8.4%)
Micro-cap with some theoretical room to re-rate if operations scale
key_risks: ROE of 0.38% signals no competitive moat and terrible capital productivity
Agri-commodity wholesaling is a low-margin, price-taker business
Incorporated 2021 — no multi-year track record of high ROIC
red_flags: ROE 0.38% — effectively destroys capital vs. risk-free rate of ~7%
Promoter holding 98.92% = near-zero float, illiquid, governance risk
Market cap INR 44.6 Cr suggests SME-tier disclosures and shallow diligence
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks companies on two axes: earnings yield (cheap) and return on capital (good). Stanbik Agro fails decisively on the second. An ROE of 0.38% is a catastrophic number — it is not a business earning high returns on incremental capital; it is a business barely generating any return at all. Even if I cannot compute EBIT/Invested Capital directly, an ROE this low makes it mathematically impossible for ROIC to be attractive. Agri-commodity wholesaling is inherently a thin-margin, working-capital-heavy business with no pricing power, so the low return is structural rather than cyclical.

On the valuation side, a P/E of 11.9 yields an earnings yield of roughly 8.4% — decent but not "bargain-bin," and certainly not cheap enough to rescue a business compounding at sub-1% on equity. Combine that with 98.92% promoter holding (essentially no public float, illiquid, prone to price manipulation) and a 2021 incorporation date (no cycle-tested track record), and this is exactly the kind of name the systematic Magic Formula screen would reject. Avoid.
